opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few layers to why it's still so hard.

The first is about what a Nobel-level discovery actually is. Most of the big ones weren't about fitting existing data better. They were about asking a question nobody thought to ask, or noticing that an anomaly everyone else dismissed was actually the important thing. Today's AI systems are extraordinarily good at interpolation, at finding structure inside the distribution of data we've already collected. A truly breakthrough discovery often sits outside that distribution. It's a change of frame, not just a better answer within the old frame.

The second layer is data. In language, we had the whole internet. In science, the data that matters is often scarce, expensive, noisy, and siloed. A single good experimental dataset in biology or materials science can take years and millions of dollars to produce. And a lot of the most valuable knowledge, the failed experiments, the tacit lab know-how, never gets published at all. So the models learn from a very biased slice of reality: mostly the successes, written up in a polished way.

Third, science isn't just thinking, it's a loop. You hypothesize, you design an experiment, you run it, you get a messy result, you revise. AI has gotten good at the hypothesis part and sometimes the analysis part, but closing the loop with the physical world is still slow. The wet lab doesn't run at GPU speed. Until we have much tighter integration between models and automated experimentation, the AI is kind of a brilliant theorist who can't touch the bench.

Fourth is verification and taste. In math or code, you can check whether an answer is right. In much of science, you can't verify a novel claim cheaply, and the space of plausible-sounding hypotheses is enormous. The hard part is judgment: knowing which of a thousand ideas is worth two years of someone's life. Great scientists have that taste, built from deep intuition and many failures. We don't yet know how to train for it.

And finally, there's a human and institutional side. Even when AI produces something genuinely new, it has to be understood, trusted, and adopted by a scientific community. AlphaFold worked partly because protein structure prediction was a well-defined problem with a decades-old benchmark, CASP, and a clear scoreboard. Most frontier questions don't come with a scoreboard like that.

So I'm optimistic, but I'd frame it this way: AI is already becoming an incredible accelerator for scientists. Making the leap from accelerator to originator, the one who reframes the question, is the hard part, and it'll probably require progress on data, on autonomous experimentation, and on how these systems reason about what they don't know.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a Nobel-level discovery is almost never the kind of problem AI is currently good at, and that mismatch comes down to a few things.

First, the hard part usually isn't the step where you already know what to compute. It's figuring out which question is worth asking in the first place. When we did the magic-angle graphene work, nobody handed us a well-defined objective. There was a theoretical hint that something might happen at a particular twist angle, but whether that would turn into superconductivity, or anything interesting at all, was completely unknown. AI today is very strong when you give it a clear target and a loss function. Protein structure prediction is a beautiful example: the question was crisp, the data existed, and the answer could be scored. Most frontier discoveries don't look like that. The question itself is the discovery.

Second, the data simply doesn't exist yet. By definition, a new phenomenon is one that isn't in anyone's dataset. You can't train on the thing you're trying to find. In experimental physics, the interesting signal is often buried in what looks like noise or an artifact. Many of the most important results started with someone staring at a plot and saying, "that's strange, that shouldn't be there." A model trained to reproduce known physics will tend to treat that anomaly as an error and smooth it over, because statistically it is an outlier. A good experimentalist treats it as the most important point in the room.

Third, real discovery is deeply entangled with the physical world. In condensed matter, so much of it is craft: how you stack the layers, how clean your interface is, how you cool the sample, what failed last week and what you changed. That tacit knowledge lives in hands and in lab notebooks, not in papers. The paper describes the result after you already know it works. It leaves out the hundred attempts that taught you what matters. An AI reading the literature sees only the polished endpoint, so it's learning from a very biased sample of how science actually happens.

And finally, there's a taste problem. Choosing a direction where the payoff is a decade away, where the current consensus says it probably won't work, and still committing to it, is a judgment call about what is important rather than what is likely. Current systems are optimized to be likely. They interpolate well within what humans have already explored, and that's genuinely useful for accelerating the middle of the process. But the breakthroughs tend to come from the edges, where the prior is weak and the reward is uncertain.

So I don't think it's impossible in principle. I think we'll first see AI dramatically compress the time between a good idea and a confirmed result, and that alone will change the pace of science. But the spark, deciding that a weird kink in the data is a door rather than a mistake, is still mostly human for now. The day an AI system insists on an anomaly that everyone else wants to throw away, and turns out to be right, that's when I'd say we're getting close.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part is that a major scientific discovery usually requires more than solving a problem we already know how to formulate. You have to notice something unexpected, recognize that it matters, and figure out what question you should be asking.

AI is very powerful when the objective is clear. If you can specify what property you want to optimize and provide a reliable way to evaluate the result, it can help you search much faster. But in fundamental research, the objective itself often changes as you learn. An experiment gives you a strange signal, and you don’t know whether it’s noise, a problem with the apparatus, or a hint of new physics. Deciding which possibility to pursue is a big part of discovery.

There’s also a data problem. We tend to record and publish the results that worked. Much of the knowledge about what failed, what was difficult to reproduce, or why a measurement might be misleading stays with the researchers. So the scientific literature doesn’t capture the entire process that produced it.

I wouldn’t say AI can’t make that kind of discovery. But making it useful for discovery requires a much tighter connection between proposing ideas, doing experiments, and revising its understanding. Producing a plausible hypothesis is one step. Establishing that nature actually behaves that way is the harder part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that a Nobel Prize-level discovery usually requires more than finding a better answer to a well-defined problem. Often, the key is realizing that we have been asking the wrong question, or noticing something that doesn’t fit our existing understanding and taking it seriously.

AI is very powerful when we can define the objective clearly and provide enough useful data. But in frontier science, we often don’t know what the important variables are, what data we should collect, or even what a good answer would look like. Those choices are part of the discovery itself.

And then there’s the experimental side. An unexpected result could be new physics, but it could also be a faulty instrument or a problem with the sample. You have to design experiments that distinguish those possibilities. That requires a continual back-and-forth between ideas and observations, rather than simply producing a plausible explanation.

So I wouldn’t say AI cannot make that kind of discovery. But the challenge is to move from recognizing patterns in what we already know to proposing something genuinely new, testing it, and establishing why we should believe it.
